role: Own continuing primary-source adjudicator; amendment, not another fresh vote.
literal_question: Before compensation starts, may you legally play a reinforcement to remove it from your hand? Once Hacker has targeted your hand, may you then dump it, and what kinds of effects can interrupt the hand-targeting action?
reader_input_boundary: The reader receives only this literal question. The fixed expected record and its contextual qualifier are background for the assignment, not words or scenario facts supplied to the reader.
scope_confidence: Moderate to high as an interpretation of this generic timing question; the published timing rules themselves are explicit. This is not a ruling on the unresolved underlying card-type legality.

literal_only_answer.first_clause: You may play it during its normal legal reinforcement-play opportunity before compensation begins. Before compensation is not, by itself, enough: it creates no new play opportunity. The question does not give enough facts to declare a particular reinforcement play legal.
literal_only_answer.second_clause: Once Hacker has targeted your hand, you cannot then dump the reinforcement through ordinary play; the earlier opportunity to affect encounter totals has passed.
literal_only_answer.third_clause: Only a Zap or a power/effect specifically allowing interruption can interrupt the hand-targeting action.

changed_reasoning.former: The first-clause answer was supported in part by the task explicitly supplying the normal-window qualifier.
changed_reasoning.change: Withdraw that support. The qualifier is not part of the reader’s question and cannot establish otherwise-legal-play as a given.

changed_reasoning.former: The prior question-scope explanation referred to the literal question and its supplied contextual qualifier together, including the claim that the task explicitly supplies that qualifier.
changed_reasoning.change: Replace this with an assessment of the literal alone. Its three linked clauses concern early versus late play and interruption; no role, revealed-card pair, or exact earlier instant is specified.

changed_reasoning.former: The earlier answer could be read as applying to a scenario already given as otherwise legally playable.
changed_reasoning.change: No such scenario premise is imported. Normal-window and other legality requirements are conditions stated in the answer, not facts presumed of a specific play.

changed_reasoning.former: The broad conclusion called the fixed timing answer complete under the supplied qualifier.
changed_reasoning.change: The conclusion is now narrower: a conditional general timing answer is complete for the literal’s general timing request, but it is not a concrete or unconditional first-clause legality determination.

literal_only_scope_reasoning: The question asks generically about before compensation, contrasts that with after Hacker targets the hand, and asks what can interrupt. It supplies no concrete card pair, role, or exact earlier play instant.

A general question about permission can be answered by stating its limits. Saying only during the normal legal opportunity answers the timing permission without assuming that opportunity is currently open.

The word legally asks for lawful play; it does not assert that any specified play is lawful. It also does not ask which revealed-card pairs qualify. The answer must therefore avoid an unqualified yes.

The direct FAQ passage itself gives the same before-compensation reinforcement example subject to cards that may legally be played. Its explicit Hacker and interruption answers explain the literal’s later clauses.

Because no concrete otherwise-legal premise is supplied, one cannot infer that this player can actually make such a play at an arbitrary pre-compensation instant. That limitation is included in the first-clause answer.
Neither clause requires deciding attack-versus-negotiate or both-negotiate reinforcement legality. Introducing a specific such pair as the reader’s intended scenario would add missing facts.

Ordinary compensation’s attack-versus-negotiate origin is a source fact, but the first clause does not specify an actual encounter or ask for all eligibility conditions in every compensation-producing scenario. Treating it as an unconditional assertion about every such encounter would enlarge the question.
Thus the literal does not necessarily demand resolving the FAQ conflict. It supports a conditional timing rule while leaving concrete card-type eligibility unresolved.

source_legal_facts_unchanged.locator: 2008 rulebook p.13, Reinforcement Cards; extract lines 1034–1046
source_legal_facts_unchanged.quote:
Instead, during the Reveal
Phase, after encounter cards are revealed, the offense, defense,
and any allies may play reinforcement cards on either side of
the encounter
source_legal_facts_unchanged.fact: The ordinary reinforcement opportunity is a defined Reveal-phase opportunity with participating roles. It is not any arbitrary moment before compensation.

source_legal_facts_unchanged.locator: 2008 rulebook p.13, Reinforcement Cards; extract lines 1043–1046
source_legal_facts_unchanged.quote:
Players may continue playing reinforcements in
response to other reinforcements until all players pass. Once all
players have passed on the opportunity to play further rein-
forcements, the encounter is resolved with the new totals.
source_legal_facts_unchanged.fact: The reinforcement opportunity closes before resolution of the encounter under these ordinary timing instructions.

source_legal_facts_unchanged.locator: 2008 rulebook p.10, attack versus negotiate; extract lines 780–786, and p.11 Compensation, lines 887–895
source_legal_facts_unchanged.quote:
When one player plays a negotiate and his opponent plays an
attack card, the player who played the negotiate card gets to
collect compensation.
source_legal_facts_unchanged.fact: Ordinary compensation is distinct from computing attack totals and is described in Resolution. This ordinary source setting does not by itself resolve the conflicting FAQ reinforcement-type permissions.

source_legal_facts_unchanged.locator: Official FAQ p.3; extract lines 238–252, particularly 241–246
source_legal_facts_unchanged.quote:
You are free to use any cards that may be 
legally played before compensation begins to be collected. So, you 
could play a reinforcement card to get it out of your hand before 
compensation is taken, for instance.
source_legal_facts_unchanged.fact: The source itself predicates the pre-compensation example on cards that may legally be played. It does not create blanket legality from the words before compensation.

source_legal_facts_unchanged.quote:
However, once the 
opportunity to play such cards has passed and compensation 
begins, then it is too late. For example, you cannot wait to see if 
Hacker is going to target you before deciding whether to “dump” 
your reinforcement cards, because the time to affect encounter 
totals has already passed.
source_legal_facts_unchanged.fact: The exact Hacker reinforcement-dumping example answers the late-play portion explicitly, independently of deciding which revealed card combinations permit a reinforcement in the earlier window.

source_legal_facts_unchanged.quote:
Once an effect targets your hand, 
nothing can interrupt that effect except a Zap or some other 
power or effect that specifically lets you interrupt it.
source_legal_facts_unchanged.fact: The permitted exception class for interruption is explicit.

source_legal_facts_unchanged.quote:
Other than playing a Zap of some kind, or an effect that 
specifically allows you to interrupt an action, no. You must 
complete an effect before executing another one.
source_legal_facts_unchanged.fact: The immediately preceding generic interruption answer agrees with the hand-targeting rule.

primary_conflict_preserved.p3_quote:
Yes, any player involved in the encounter may play a 
reinforcement on either side, regardless of what type of encounter 
cards were revealed.
primary_conflict_preserved.p3_question_scope: The preceding question explicitly includes attack versus negotiate and both negotiates.
primary_conflict_preserved.p4_quote:
Q: Can you play a reinforcement card on a negotiate?
A: No.
primary_conflict_preserved.status: Conflict recorded, not resolved, ranked, harmonized, or assigned to a particular side or card-type scenario.
primary_conflict_preserved.consequence: These statements can affect whether a concrete reinforcement play involving a negotiate is otherwise legal. This adjudication supplies no such concrete legality verdict.

source_vs_scope.explicit_published: Normal Reveal reinforcement opportunity, legal-play qualification before compensation, Hacker too-late example, and special interruption exceptions.
source_vs_scope.interpretive: Classifying the literal as answerable at the general timing level without a concrete eligibility adjudication is this adjudicator’s question-scope interpretation.
source_vs_scope.not_published: No official statement says Q074 is independent of the conflict; Q074 is the supplied local literal, not a published FAQ identifier.

limitations_and_dependency_boundary.underlying_conflict: The conflicting p.3 regardless-of-card-type and p.4 no-on-negotiate statements remain unresolved. This amendment does not interpret, harmonize, rank, or decide them.
limitations_and_dependency_boundary.when_dependency_would_arise: If the requested first-clause answer were required to be an unconditional yes/no for a specified negotiate-containing encounter, or a claim that every pre-compensation reinforcement play is legal, this conditional answer would not establish that claim; concrete eligibility would need further facts and potentially resolution of the source conflict.
limitations_and_dependency_boundary.what_is_complete: The general before/after timing and interruption answer, including the explicit limitation that before-compensation alone confers no play permission.
limitations_and_dependency_boundary.what_is_not_complete: A complete catalogue of all reinforcement eligibility conditions or a concrete legality ruling absent from the literal.
limitations_and_dependency_boundary.no_claims: No global bank PASS, score, audit, freeze, full-source inspection, new fresh vote, or peer opinion.
